config.title: Build typed nav schema and guards

intro.title: Build typed nav schema and guards
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a typed navigation schema and guard functions to safely manage routes in a TypeScript application. You'll learn how to define a set of allowed routes as a union type, creating a single source of truth for your app's navigation. Using this schema, you will implement guard functions that use type narrowing to check if a given string is a valid route before navigating. This approach ensures type safety, prevents runtime errors, and provides better developer experience through autocompletion and error checking.
intro.usecase: This pattern is essential for building robust navigation systems in enterprise applications like admin dashboards, e-commerce platforms, and SaaS products. For example, in a banking dashboard, typed navigation schemas ensure users can only access routes appropriate to their role (customer vs. admin), while guards prevent unauthorized access to sensitive financial data pages. Developers implement these to create maintainable, type-safe navigation structures that prevent runtime errors and enforce business rules across complex multi-view applications.

objectives: Construct a TypeScript type definition for a navigation schema with typed routes.
Initialize a constant object that implements the navigation schema type.
Implement a type guard function to validate route objects at runtime.
Apply the type guard within a conditional block to control program flow.
Manipulate the navigation schema to add a new typed route property.
Integrate the navigation schema and guard into a simple route-checking utility.

steps.title: Import TypeScript and define navigation route types
steps.instruction: Create a type definition for navigation routes with home, about, and contact routes, each having required and optional parameters.
steps.hint: Define a TypeScript type or interface that represents different route objects with properties like id, path, and params.

steps.expectedOutcome: A TypeScript type definition that can be used to type-check navigation routes throughout the application.
successCriteria: A type or interface named something like NavRoute or Route is defined with properties for id, path, and params (with required and optional fields).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your type includes properties for id, path, and params with both required and optional fields.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try defining a TypeScript type or interface with properties like id (string), path (string), and params (an object with some required and optional fields).

steps.title: Define the navigation schema interface
steps.instruction: Create an interface named NavigationSchema that maps route names (as string keys) to their corresponding route types (the Route type you defined earlier).
steps.hint: Think of NavigationSchema as a blueprint for your entire navigation system. Use the Route type as the value type for each route name key.

steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a structured NavigationSchema interface that defines the shape of your navigation system.
successCriteria: The NavigationSchema interface is defined with string index signature mapping to Route type.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your interface has the correct name and properly maps string keys to the Route type.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try again. You need to create an interface named NavigationSchema that maps route names (strings) to Route types.

steps.title: Create the concrete navigation schema object
steps.instruction: Create a constant named navigationSchema that satisfies the NavigationSchema interface. Define it with at least one route object containing path and metadata properties.
steps.hint: Use the 'const' keyword to declare navigationSchema and assign it an object that matches the NavigationSchema interface structure you defined earlier.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a typed navigationSchema object that implements your NavigationSchema interface with actual route data.
successCriteria: A constant named navigationSchema is declared and assigned an object with at least one route that includes path and metadata properties, satisfying the NavigationSchema interface.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure navigationSchema is a constant with an object that matches the NavigationSchema interface structure.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you've declared a constant named navigationSchema with an object containing route configurations that include path and metadata.

steps.title: Define type guards for route validation
steps.instruction: Create three type guard functions: isHomeRoute, isAboutRoute, and isContactRoute. Each should take a parameter of type Route and return a boolean indicating if it matches that specific route type.
steps.hint: Type guard functions use the 'is' keyword in their return type annotation to help TypeScript narrow types. For example: function isHomeRoute(route: Route): route is HomeRoute { return route.path === '/home'; }
steps.expectedOutcome: Three type guard functions that can validate whether a given Route object matches specific route types.
successCriteria: isHomeRoute, isAboutRoute, and isContactRoute functions are defined with proper type annotations and return boolean values based on route properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created some type guards, but make sure all three functions (isHomeRoute, isAboutRoute, isContactRoute) are defined with proper return type annotations using the 'is' keyword.
steps.feedbackWrong: Type guard functions are missing or incorrectly defined. Each function should take a Route parameter and return a boolean with a type predicate like 'route is HomeRoute'.

steps.title: Create a generic route validation function
steps.instruction: Create a function named validateRoute that takes a route object and returns a boolean indicating if it's a valid route according to your schema.
steps.hint: Use your type guard functions inside validateRoute to check the route object's properties.
steps.expectedOutcome: A validateRoute function that leverages your type guards to validate any route object.
successCriteria: validateRoute function is defined and uses the type guard functions to check route validity.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but make sure it uses your type guard functions to validate the route object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The validateRoute function is missing or doesn't properly use the type guards for validation.

steps.title: Define the main App component structure
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns a JSX element. Use TypeScript to explicitly annotate the return type as JSX.Element.
steps.hint: Define a component that returns a simple JSX element like a <div> with some text content.
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional App component with proper TypeScript return type annotation is defined.
successCriteria: App component is defined as a function with explicit JSX.Element return type and returns a JSX element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a component, but check if it has the correct return type annotation (JSX.Element).
steps.feedbackWrong: The App component isn't properly defined. Make sure to create a function named App that returns JSX with explicit return type.

steps.title: Initialize component state for current route
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, initialize a state variable named 'currentRoute' using useState. The state should be typed with the NavigationSchema interface and initialized with the 'home' route from your navigationSchema object.
steps.hint: Use useState with a generic type parameter to specify the state type. Import useState from 'react' if you haven't already.
steps.expectedOutcome: The App component will have a typed state variable that tracks the current navigation route, initialized to the 'home' route.
successCriteria: The useState hook is called with the NavigationSchema type and initialized with navigationSchema.home
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to: 1) Use the NavigationSchema type for the state, 2) Initialize it with navigationSchema.home, and 3) Name the state variable 'currentRoute'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The state initialization is missing or incorrect. You need to use useState with the NavigationSchema type and initialize it with the 'home' route from your navigationSchema object.

steps.title: Create navigation handler functions
steps.instruction: Inside your App component, create three navigation handler functions: navigateToHome, navigateToAbout, and navigateToContact. Each function should call the validateRoute function with the appropriate route name and update the currentRoute state with the validated result.
steps.hint: Define each function using either function declarations or arrow functions. Inside each function, call validateRoute with a route name like 'home', 'about', or 'contact', then use setCurrentRoute with the result.
steps.expectedOutcome: Three navigation handler functions are defined inside the App component, each validating a specific route and updating the currentRoute state.
successCriteria: The navigateToHome, navigateToAbout, and navigateToContact functions are defined, each calling validateRoute with the correct route name and using setCurrentRoute with the result.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created some navigation handlers, but make sure you have all three: navigateToHome, navigateToAbout, and navigateToContact. Each should validate its route and update state.
steps.feedbackWrong: The navigation handlers aren't properly defined. Create three functions that validate routes and update the currentRoute state.

steps.title: Build the navigation UI structure
steps.instruction: Inside your component's return statement, add a <nav> element containing buttons for each route defined in your navigation schema (Home, About, Contact).
steps.hint: Place the <nav> element after the <h1> tag. Each button should have a descriptive label matching the route name.
steps.expectedOutcome: A navigation bar with three buttons (Home, About, Contact) appears below the main heading.
successCriteria: The component returns a <nav> element containing three <button> elements with appropriate labels.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you have exactly three buttons (Home, About, Contact) inside the <nav> element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The navigation UI structure is incomplete. Add a <nav> element with three buttons for the Home, About, and Contact routes.
